references.text: The immediate context: the Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod intends to kill him. Jesus responds by calling Herod a "fox" ([ref:Luk 13:31|Luke 13:31]).
Jesus continues by saying that a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem – this links his "completion" on the third day to his impending suffering in Jerusalem ([ref:Luk 13:33|Luke 13:33]).
Herod Antipas is also mentioned in connection with his fear of Jesus and his deeds, which sheds light on the background of the threats against Jesus ([ref:Mark 6:14-16|Mark 6:14-16]).
Herod's interest in Jesus and desire to see him are noted, showing the political threat Jesus faced ([ref:Luk 9:7-9|Luke 9:7-9]).
Jesus predicts his suffering, death, and resurrection on the third day. The phrase "on the third day" in Luke 13:32 points forward to the resurrection ([ref:Luk 9:22|Luke 9:22]).
Jesus again predicts his suffering and resurrection on the third day, consistent with the words about being "completed" ([ref:Luk 18:31-33|Luke 18:31-33]).
"After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up" – a prophetic text that connects to the theme of the third day and the completion Jesus speaks of ([ref:Hos 6:2|Hosea 6:2]).
The term "τελειοῦμαι" (to be completed/perfected) is also used in Hebrews regarding Jesus, who was made perfect through suffering ([ref:Hebr 2:10|Hebrews 2:10]).
Jesus was "completed" (τελειωθείς) and became the source of eternal salvation – this elaborates on what it means for Jesus to "complete" his work ([ref:Hebr 5:9|Hebrews 5:9]).
Jesus speaks of having completed (τελειόω) the work the Father gave him to do. This clarifies what Jesus means by being "completed" in Luke 13:32 ([ref:Joh 17:4|John 17:4]).
Jesus' words "It is finished" (τετέλεσται) on the cross connect to the completion he mentions in Luke 13:32 ([ref:Joh 19:30|John 19:30]).
Jesus drives out evil spirits by the Spirit of God as a sign that the kingdom of God has come – this sheds light on Jesus' mention of casting out demons ([ref:Matt 12:28|Matthew 12:28]).
Jesus' programmatic speech in Nazareth, where he declares his mission of healing and liberation – this is the foundation for the ministry he refers to in Luke 13:32 ([ref:Luk 4:18-19|Luke 4:18-19]).
